An aide-mémoire is anything — most often a written document or a physical object — that helps you remember something you might otherwise forget. Think of it as a personal memory assistant: you create or use it precisely because your unaided memory isn't reliable enough for a particular purpose.

In ordinary life, an aide-mémoire is any kind of reminder or memory aid. A shopping list is an aide-mémoire. So is a sticky note on your computer screen saying "call the dentist," a string tied around your finger, or a quick voice memo on your phone. What all of these share is a single purpose: they exist to jog your memory so you don't drop the ball on something important.

In this sense, the word is broader than "note" or "list" — it covers anything that performs the function of reminding, regardless of its form.

In more formal settings — especially in diplomacy, business, law, and government — an aide-mémoire is a specific kind of written document. Here it has a precise meaning:

It is a brief, written summary of the key points of a discussion, meeting, negotiation, or proposal, prepared so that all parties involved can refer back to it later and confirm that they share the same understanding of what was said or agreed upon.

Imagine two government ministers meeting to discuss a trade deal. After the meeting, one side sends the other a concise written record of the main points covered — what was proposed, what was tentatively agreed, what still needs to be resolved. That document is an aide-mémoire. It isn't a binding contract or a formal treaty. It is less official and less legally weighty than those. Its purpose is to keep everyone on the same page, prevent misremembering or misrepresentation, and serve as a reference point going forward.

In diplomacy, aide-mémoires are frequently exchanged between foreign ministries and embassies. They are usually written in the third person (e.g., "The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Country X wishes to draw attention to...") and are kept on file as a record of communication.

In business, an aide-mémoire might be distributed after a strategy meeting, summarising the decisions taken and the action points assigned. In legal and policy work, it might be a concise brief that a lawyer or official prepares for someone who needs to quickly grasp the essential points of a complex matter without reading the full original documents.

Whether you're talking about a sticky note on your fridge or a diplomatic memorandum exchanged between two nations, the concept is always the same: an aide-mémoire is a tool that does the work of memory for you. It captures important information in a retrievable form so that nothing is forgotten, distorted, or disputed.

The word signals something more deliberate and considered than a casual scribble — it implies that the information being recorded is significant enough that forgetting it would matter.

• Before the presentation, she prepared a brief aide-mémoire listing the three main arguments she wanted to make.
  • The two governments exchanged an aide-mémoire outlining the terms discussed during the bilateral talks.
  • He kept an aide-mémoire of his doctor's instructions stuck to the bathroom mirror.
  • The ambassador's aide-mémoire was a formal acknowledgement that the meeting had taken place and these points had been raised.

Tone and register: The word has a slightly formal, educated tone. You would not typically hear someone say "my grocery list is my aide-mémoire" in casual speech — they'd just say "reminder" or "note." But in professional, academic, or diplomatic writing, aide-mémoire is used naturally and precisely.

Plural: The plural is either aides-mémoire (following the French pattern) or aide-mémoires (following the English pattern). Both are acceptable in English; you'll see both in formal writing.

The key distinction from similar words: A memo is an internal communication within an organisation. A minutes document is a formal record of everything discussed in a meeting. A briefing note is a summary prepared to inform someone before an event. An aide-mémoire overlaps with all of these but is specifically defined by its purpose — it exists to preserve memory and ensure accurate recall, not primarily to inform or instruct someone who wasn't present.

In short: if something exists mainly to make sure you (or someone else) doesn't forget what was said, decided, or agreed — whether it's a handwritten note or a formal diplomatic paper — it is an aide-mémoire.
